extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and working humor writers, comedians, and creators (writers of fiction, comedy, memoir, essays, narrative nonfiction, copywriters)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing comedy and satire, developing a distinctive comedic voice/brand, generating material, editing jokes, and building an audience across media. Includes practical tools (clown vs. editor brain, morning pages, funny filters) and career-minded guidance (persistence, self-publishing vs. gatekeepers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding and developing a consistent comedic voice/brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover and refine a single, recognizable voice — e.g., The Onion’s deadpan AP journalism parody — through experimentation and concentrated direction once the grain of the voice is identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It was a glacial R&D process over years involving many formats (radio, ads, TV pilots). Make many experiments, learn from mistakes, then focus ('direct all firepower') on the style that fits. Branding emerges after sustained trial-and-error rather than instantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of format-as-parody / conceit (masquerade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a conceit (e.g., a humor publication masquerading as a newspaper) that shapes tone and comedic possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong conceit gives rules and constraints that can heighten comedy (deadpan delivery, straight reading). Use format-specific strengths (e.g., parodying AM-radio or classified ads) to create pitch-perfect pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t wait for permission — be proactively distributive
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t need gatekeepers to start; show up, send unsolicited work, self-publish, and use modern platforms (blogs, podcasts, YouTube) to build an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical tactic: send unsolicited comics/newspapers. Today: be all over every platform, repeatedly push work into the world. Anti-pattern: passively waiting to be discovered by gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue both building-your-own-work and traditional gatekeeper opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do both self-production and pursue establishment opportunities — each path has benefits and they reinforce each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early on you may only be able to self-produce; that’s fine. Being active on both increases chances: self-made projects attract bigger opportunities; don’t only wait for a network or publisher to grant access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantity to achieve quality / over-generate material
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate large volumes (hundreds of headlines/ideas/drafts) rather than expecting a perfect first draft or solitary genius moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unleash the ‘clown brain’ to over-produce, then switch to the ‘editor brain’ to select and refine. Tools include morning pages, free writing, and habitually jotting ideas. Example: inventing hundreds of headlines to find the best ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and balance Clown Brain vs Editor Brain; be dextrous switching between them
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate an unfiltered creative mode (clown) for idea generation and a critical mode (editor) for selection and honing; ability to switch rapidly is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clown brain = no filter, endless play; Editor brain = critique, Funny Filters, refinement. Over-reliance on Editor = writer’s block. Develop both (tools described in How to Write Funny) and practice switching so you can produce under deadlines and self-edit when no team is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools to develop Clown Brain (morning pages, jotting, free writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use routines that prime uninhibited idea generation: morning pages, jotting ideas in a notebook, and habitual free writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices build muscle for clown-brain output so you can produce many raw materials quickly. Anti-pattern: waiting for inspiration or attempting perfection on the first pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tools to develop Editor Brain (11 Funny Filters, structured feedback, best practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and apply specific editorial filters and best practices (e.g., the book’s '11 Funny Filters') and learn how to get useful feedback from readers/peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practiced filters to evaluate what's funniest and to refine premises; solicit constructive feedback deliberately (see How to Write Funnier methods). Editor training reduces noise and aids reliable selection of material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three methods of joke creation: Filtering, Finessing, Divining
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply systematic methods (Filtering, Finessing, Divining) to create and refine jokes rather than relying solely on intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural approaches described in HTWF (How to Write Funny) to move from raw clown output to polished comedic work; use them to structure editing sessions and to get more predictable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist editing questions used in writers’ rooms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific evaluative questions during editing: 'What’s this saying?'; 'Is this the best joke that can be made about this subject?'; 'Yeah but will it make people laugh?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concise, outcome-focused questions help keep pieces aimed at clarity, maximal joke-making, and audience response. In improv/use-case formats also ask: 'What’s the game of this scene?' and 'If this is true, what else is true?' For conceptual writing: 'What’s the main premise?' and 'Is this heightening enough?'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make subtext substantive, accessible, and layered
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for subtext that comments substantially on the world (satire) and is objectively relatable while allowing layers that different audiences can access at different depths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire’s subtext should convey deep truths; not all readers must get every layer — groundlings can laugh at surface jokes while 'kings' appreciate subtext. As a creator, articulate and test your subtext to ensure it's intelligible and resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied transparency of subtext is acceptable — broad appeal and layered meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that highest-level satire can be widely funny even if only some readers perceive deeper subtext; pieces can function on multiple levels simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pieces so surface humor works for general audiences, with subtler subtext for sophisticated readers. Anti-pattern: making subtext so obscure that it fails even for the intended 'kings'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence, deliberate practice, and iterative improvement over innate talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize sustained hard work, practice, and iterative improvement — talent is learned, not fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most successful writers started with little experience and improved through sustained effort. Evaluate potential by work ethic and improvement trajectory rather than presumed innate ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and professional traits that predict success
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued traits include loving the work, being pleasant to work with, reliability, openness to criticism, and seeking mentorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hiring or collaborating, Scott favored people who worked hard and were coachable and reliable. Anti-patterns: gifted-but-entitled creators who don’t do the labor to improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to change approach; measure forward progress vs. when to quit
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between projects that need more time/iteration and those that truly aren’t working by assessing small forward progress, sharpening of work, and whether you still love the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you love the work and see even incremental improvement, continue and change tactics when necessary. If you don’t love it, the long slog is unlikely to be rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to produce on demand and self-trust when team feedback is unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to crank out usable drafts quickly ('produce on a dime') and trust your Editor brain when you can’t access a team for feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice switching brains so you can meet tight deadlines. Train the Editor brain sufficiently (filters, feedback experience) so it can be trusted in solo editing situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental R&D across media and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore many formats (radio, in-house ads, TV pilots, podcasts, books) as experiments to discover what works and to refine voice and techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Onion’s varied experiments helped locate and sharpen its voice. Use cross-platform experimentation as feedback and learning rather than treating any single format as definitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in business and marketing skills to support creative projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn marketing, business, and platform skills (ads, self-publishing, analytics) to successfully build and sustain creative projects and reach audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scott spent on courses in business/marketing because creative success also requires distribution and monetization skills; don’t assume editorial skill alone will build the venture.
